boundary_note: Bounded first pass for Bodart's Herbrechtingen entry (16 October 1805) in cohort v1's third-coalition 1805 group: Murat's pursuit force (Dupont's division, Klein's dragoon division, the Guard chasseurs and light cavalry) against Werneck's corps of the Austrian army, from the French attack near Albeck on the 16th to the capture of Herbrechtingen that night. Bodart does not say whether his entry covers the day's pursuit or only the night action at Herbrechtingen; both are recorded and kept apart where the sources allow. The action at Albeck on 15 October and Werneck's retreat on the 17th (B365b) are context. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.value: Bodart gives side A (French) 8,000 men under Marshal Prince Murat and side B (Austrian) 4,000 men under FML Prince Hohenzollern. By his stated rule these are the forces available for the engagement, rounded up.
claims.rationale: Bodart's printed entry, read from the page image in the frame transcription; one claim among several. He does not say which formations he counted, nor whether the entry covers the day's pursuit from Albeck or only the night action at Herbrechtingen. Side A's own information gives about 8,000 men for the Austrian rearguard (claim side-b-french-figures), the figure Bodart prints for side A; Krauss gives Werneck's corps in battalions and squadrons only (claim krauss-side-b-columns). The passages read do not say which figures Bodart used. English rendering (ours) of Bodart's rules: p. 46, 'the strengths given are always those forces that were disposable for the battle'; p. 47, 'the strength and loss figures were rounded up by the author'. English rendering (ours) of the entry: 'victory of the French (8,000 men) under Marshal Prince Murat over the Austrians (4,000 men) under FML Prince Hohenzollern'.

claims.value: Side A's returns at the crossing of the Rhine, in the first days of vendémiaire year XIV (late September 1805), list the 6th corps' 1st division as the 9e légère (2 battalions, 1,763 men), 32e de ligne (2, 1,662) and 96e (2, 1,721), 6 battalions and 5,146 men by our sum, and the corps' 1er hussards as 3 squadrons, 375 men and 408 troop horses; the 5th corps' 13e and 21e chasseurs as 3 squadrons each, with 339 and 331 men and 347 and 344 troop horses; and the cavalry reserve's 1re division de dragons as the 1er, 2e, 20e, 4e, 14e and 26e dragons, 18 squadrons, 2,489 men and 2,362 troop horses by our sum. The returns' totals are headed 'présents sous les armes' (present under arms). Krauss says Napoleon assigned Murat Dupont's division with the 1st hussars, Klein's dragoon division, the Guard chasseurs à cheval and the two carabinier regiments of Nansouty's division, and that Murat also drew in the two chasseur regiments of the 5th corps (Fauconnet's brigade). The day after the action, at Neresheim, Alombert and Colin give Klein's division as 1800 horses and five guns, and Krauss as 1800 riders and 5 guns.
claims.rationale: Side A's own figures for the formations the passages name in the action, read from the page images. The returns are some three weeks older than the action and show neither detachments nor the losses of the march and of the actions fought since, among them Haslach (draft B363c) and Albeck the day before; their total, 8,680 men by our sum, is therefore not the strength on 16 October. The returns print no division subtotals, so 5,146, 2,489 and 2,362 are our sums. Dupont's division is matched to the 6th corps' 1st division by its regiments: the 9e léger took Herbrechtingen, and Murat's letter (OCR) has Dupont bivouac with the 32e and 96e. Klein's division is matched to the 1re division de dragons by that division's journal, which narrates Klein's action (OCR), and by the 20e dragons. The two chasseur regiments are numbered only in the OCR passages. The strength of the Guard chasseurs was not found; the carabiniers' rows are not cited because no passage read shows them engaged (Murat's letter has them bivouac with Dupont). The 1800 horses of the next day are a figure after this action, not added. Most of the force was assigned by Napoleon's verbal order and Berthier's order to Dupont (claim side-a-command); Krauss says Murat drew in the two chasseur regiments himself, while Alombert and Colin say they came with Oudinot's grenadiers and the journal that Murat attached them to the dragoons, so the boundary for that part is not established and the claim is tagged unresolved. English renderings (ours): '6th army corps', '5th army corps' and 'cavalry reserve at the crossing of the Rhine in the first days of vendémiaire year XIV'; 'total of those present under arms'; Krauss, 'as troops there were assigned to him: Dupont's division with the 1st hussar regiment and Klein's dragoon division, which already stood at Albeck, the Guard chasseurs à cheval and the two carabinier regiments of Nansouty's division, which had already been directed on Albeck'; 'also drew in the two chasseur regiments of the 5th corps (General Fauconnet's brigade)'; Murat, 'General Dupont went to bivouac at the village of Bissingen, with the two carabinier regiments and the 32nd and 96th infantry'; the journal, 'marches and historical reports of the 1st division of mounted dragoons'; 'and the 1st dragoon division (to which Prince Murat had joined the 13th and 21st chasseur regiments, detached from General Oudinot's division)'; Alombert and Colin, 'the 13th and 21st chasseurs, come with Oudinot's grenadiers'; 'determined General Klein to attack him with his division alone, 1800 horses and five guns strong'; Krauss, 'the division counted 1800 riders and 5 guns'.

claims.value: Side B (Austrian) in Krauss: FML Werneck had his corps march off on the 15th in two columns, 11 battalions and 10 squadrons under FML Count Hohenzollern by Hermaringen and Brenz on Langenau, and 12 battalions and 13 squadrons under FML Count Baillet de Latour by Hausen and Nerenstetten on Albeck; after the action at Albeck a detachment of 2 battalions and 2 squadrons under GM Dienersberg was directed on Langenau. On the 16th both columns met at Herbrechtingen at 5 in the afternoon.
claims.rationale: Side B's own history, read from the page images; Krauss gives no headcount for the corps before the action. The columns are as they marched on the 15th, and the passages read do not say how many battalions and squadrons were left on the morning of the 16th or which of them stood at Herbrechtingen, so they are not added; the losses of the day are in claim side-b-losses-reported. Krauss's note that the corps had scarcely 6000 men describes it on the next day's march, after this action. The corps' composition was set before the action, so the claim is tagged inherited. English renderings (ours): 'FML Werneck therefore had his corps march off on the 15th at 11 in the morning in 2 columns, namely one column, 11 battalions and 10 squadrons strong, under FML Count Hohenzollern by Hermaringen and Brenz on Langenau, the other, 12 battalions and 13 squadrons, under FML Count Baillet de Latour by Hausen and Nerenstetten on Albeck'; 'a detachment under GM Dienersberg, 2 battalions and 2 squadrons, was directed on Langenau'; 'at 5 in the afternoon both of Werneck's columns met at Herbrechtingen'; 'the corps had scarcely 6000 men'.

claims.value: Side B (Austrian), side A's figures: Alombert and Colin say that by the information Dupont's aide de camp, chef de bataillon de Conchy, sent the Emperor that evening, the troops Murat beat were a rearguard of about 8,000 men under General Werneck, belonging to a corps of 15,000 to 20,000 men commanded by Hohenlohe. Murat wrote that the enemy had taken position at Herbrechtingen with the rest of its infantry and much artillery, and the next day that five enemy cavalry regiments were fleeing before him.
claims.rationale: Side A's estimates, read from the page images except the cavalry regiments, seen in the OCR ('cinq' is printed as a word). Conchy's information names the corps' commander as Hohenlohe, where Krauss has Werneck commanding the corps (claim side-b-command). Not combined with Krauss's battalions (claim krauss-side-b-columns). claims.value: In the night before the action Napoleon gave Murat at headquarters a verbal order to go to Albeck and to beat and pursue the Austrian corps Dupont had brought to bay there; Berthier sent Dupont the order to attack early, an order Alombert and Colin did not find but know from the division's journal and General Mouton's report. Murat used the parley Dupont had opened to reconnoitre the enemy (the dragoon division's journal says Murat himself suspended the fight to make proposals, which were rejected), and when the Austrian cavalry fell back on Nerenstetten he ordered General Klein to charge; Alombert and Colin say Murat led the dragoons' charge in person. Klein passed his dragoons through the tired hussars and chasseurs to continue the pursuit, and summoned Werneck to surrender. Murat then resolved to drive the enemy from Herbrechtingen, and the skirmishers of the 9e léger took the village. Murat went back to sleep at Hausen; Napoleon, answering his report, wrote that he should have spent the night where the 9th light regiment was.
claims.rationale: Decisions at the engagement from Murat's own letter, an interested account, the dragoon division's journal, Alombert and Colin and Krauss (OCR passages, except those read from the page images); the order from above and Murat's own decisions are both recorded (claim posture). Napoleon's remark is a judgment, not a measured effect. English renderings (ours): Krauss, 'in the night before 16 October, when the report of the action at Albeck had already come in, Murat received at headquarters from Napoleon the verbal order to go to Albeck and to beat and pursue the Austrian corps that Dupont had brought to bay there'; Alombert and Colin, 'Berthier sends Dupont the order to attack early'; '(1) this order has not reached us, but it is mentioned ... in the division's journal and in General Mouton's report, so as to remove any doubt'; Murat, 'I took advantage of the parley opened by General Dupont to reconnoitre his position'; the journal, 'arrived immediately afterwards and had the fighting suspended in order to make proposals, which were rejected'; Murat, 'when I saw that the cavalry was making a retrograde movement on Nerenstetten, I gave General Klein the order to charge it'; Alombert and Colin, 'Murat, who led the dragoons' charge in person, goes back to sleep at Hausen'; the journal, 'the chasseurs and hussars complaining that they were tired, General Klein, to exploit his advantage, ordered them to form to the right and left of the road, to let the dragoons pass and serve as a reserve if needed'; Krauss, 'General Klein summoned Werneck to surrender. Werneck gave no answer at all'; Murat, 'I resolved to drive the enemy from Herbrechtingen'; 'the skirmishers of the 9th light infantry attacked the village and took it'; Napoleon, as Krauss gives him, 'it seems to me that you should have spent the night at the place where the 9th light regiment was, so as to be able to follow the enemy at daybreak and overtake him'.

claims.value: FML Werneck commanded the Austrian corps; Dupont's parlementaire brought back that it was under Werneck, subordinate to Archduke Ferdinand. On the 16th Werneck decided to retreat to the Archduke at Aalen, since the march on Ulm seemed impossible to him; he began the retreat to Herbrechtingen in the morning and sent FML Count Hohenzollern orders to march there at once. He gave no answer to Klein's summons, drew up his troops on the heights of Herbrechtingen to hold up the pursuers, and after the loss of the place continued the retreat on Heidenheim that night. The dragoon division's journal names General O'Donnel as commanding the rearguard. On Werneck's report the Archduke sent him orders to fall back on Öttingen.
claims.rationale: Side B's decisions as Krauss gives them, with side A's accounts (OCR passages, except those read from the page images). Bodart names Hohenzollern as side B's commander (claim bodart-commanders). By Krauss, Werneck received the Archduke's order to march by Neresheim and Trochtelfingen to Öttingen at Ober-Kochen on the next day, after this action. English renderings (ours): Alombert and Colin, 'but he brings back the information that the enemy is commanded by General Werneck, under the orders of Archduke Ferdinand'; Krauss, 'FML Werneck therefore had his corps march off'; 'he therefore decided, and because the march on Ulm seemed impossible to him, on the retreat to Aalen to Archduke Ferdinand'; 'on Werneck's report about the action at Albeck and the impossibility of breaking through to Ulm, Archduke Ferdinand sent Werneck the order to fall back on Öttingen'; 'Werneck meanwhile had already begun the retreat to Herbrechtingen on the morning of the 16th and had also sent FML Count Hohenzollern orders to march at once to Herbrechtingen'; 'General Klein summoned Werneck to surrender. Werneck gave no answer at all'; 'Werneck now drew up his troops on the heights of Herbrechtingen to hold up the pursuing enemy'; 'Werneck continued the retreat on Heidenheim that same night'; the journal, 'General O'Donnel, commanding the rearguard'; Krauss, 'in Ober-Kochen Werneck received Archduke Ferdinand's order to march by Ebnat, Neresheim and Trochtelfingen to Öttingen'.

claims.value: Bodart records a victory of side A (French) over side B (Austrian). Krauss says Dupont's light infantry regiment took Herbrechtingen after a short fight, cutting off and capturing a considerable part of Werneck's infantry, and that Werneck continued his retreat on Heidenheim in the night; Alombert and Colin say the 9e léger, with the Guard chasseurs and the 20e dragons, carried the village and established itself there. The attack on the place came at 9 in the evening by the dragoon division's journal and Krauss, and at 11 by Murat's letter. No source read gives a different result.
claims.rationale: The frozen frame outcome, with the agreeing accounts of both sides, read from the page images; the hour of the night attack differs between accounts and is not resolved. English renderings (ours): Bodart, 'victory of the French'; Krauss, 'at 9 in the evening, however, Dupont's light infantry regiment arrived, which after a short fight took Herbrechtingen and thereby cut off and captured a considerable part of Werneck's infantry'; 'Werneck continued the retreat on Heidenheim that same night'; Alombert and Colin, 'this regiment, with the Guard chasseurs and the 20th dragoons, carries the village of Herbrechtingen and establishes itself there'; the journal, 'at 9 in the evening, the 9th light infantry regiment having arrived, we marched forward again'; Murat, 'it was 11 o'clock at night; the skirmishers of the 9th light infantry attacked the village and took it'.

claims.value: Side A's artillery could not keep up with the cavalry's rapid movements, and with night approaching the action was suspended near Eselsburg; Klein was then two long leagues ahead of the infantry. Murat wrote that Herbrechtingen was the only village offering some resources for his corps, and Alombert and Colin that the light cavalry that had led the pursuit was exhausted and gave way to the dragoons. Side B's retreat, by Krauss, went only slowly, hard pressed by French infantry and cavalry against which it repeatedly had to turn and face; in Herbrechtingen it left about twenty caissons or wagons of ammunition.
claims.rationale: Means and supply as the passages read give them (OCR passages, except those read from the page images); no ration, ammunition or horse return for 16 October was inspected. claims.value: Napoleon sent his aide de camp General Mouton to Dupont's division for reliable information. On the 16th Dupont's parlementaire brought back that the enemy was commanded by Werneck under Archduke Ferdinand, and the dragoon division's journal says Klein had reported to Murat the previous day's events and the enemy's position and forces. Murat attacked Herbrechtingen in the belief that the enemy held it only to cover the retreat of its baggage and artillery and would not stand; the next morning he did not yet know the number of prisoners. That evening Dupont's aide de camp de Conchy reported to the Emperor that the troops beaten were a rearguard under Werneck, part of a larger corps under Hohenlohe.
claims.rationale: Side A's information as its documents and Alombert and Colin give it (OCR passages, except those read from the page images); Conchy's figures are in claim side-b-french-figures. English renderings (ours): Alombert and Colin, 'he sends his aide de camp, General Mouton, to Dupont's division, so as to obtain fully reliable information'; 'but he brings back the information that the enemy is commanded by General Werneck, under the orders of Archduke Ferdinand'; the journal, 'Prince Murat, to whom General Klein had reported what had happened the day before, the position and the forces of the enemy'; Murat, 'I decided on this attack from my conviction that the enemy held there only to protect the retreat of his baggage and his artillery, and because I was convinced that the enemy, terrified by his rout, would not hold there'; 'I do not yet know the number of prisoners'; Alombert and Colin, 'according to the information sent that same evening to the Emperor by an aide de camp of General Dupont, chef de bataillon de Conchy'.

claims.value: Werneck learned from GM Mecsery of the defeat of Riesch's corps at Elchingen and that it had cut his own corps off from Ulm, news hard to reconcile with Mack's order, which stated as certain that the enemy was retreating to France; in his relation he adds that he had news of the enemy showing in strength at Ellwangen and Nördlingen. Before the retreat he received Mack's general order, which held the enemy's retreat to be beyond doubt, and the Archduke's order from Aalen, and concluded from the Archduke's presence at Aalen that the enemy's retreat had been invented. Dupont's parlementaire told him that Ulm had capitulated and invited him to do likewise.
claims.rationale: Side B's information as Krauss gives it from Werneck's report and relation, and side A's message as Alombert and Colin give it (OCR passages). Whether Ulm had capitulated when the parlementaire said so is not settled by these passages (see B365a). English renderings (ours): Krauss, 'from him Werneck learned of the changed task of Riesch's corps and its defeat at Elchingen, and that through this defeat Werneck's corps was cut off from Ulm'; 'this news could only with difficulty be brought into agreement with the content of Mack's order, "whose statement that the enemy was retreating to France bore the stamp of definite certainty"'; Werneck, 'the more so as I received news that the enemy was also showing in strength at Ellwangen and Nördlingen'; Krauss, 'which stated that the enemy's retreat was beyond doubt, and an order of Archduke Ferdinand from Aalen'; 'Werneck concluded from the Archduke's presence in Aalen that the enemy's retreat was invented'; Alombert and Colin, 'meanwhile Dupont sends a parlementaire to the commander of the enemy troops to inform him that Ulm has capitulated and invite him to do the same'.

claims.value: Werneck's relation says that, however the matter stood, he had to attack toward Langenau and Albeck to harm the retreating enemy or, if it was not retreating, to help the army in Ulm to withdraw. On the 16th he decided to retreat to Archduke Ferdinand at Aalen, and at Herbrechtingen he drew up his troops on the heights to hold up the pursuing enemy, which succeeded into the night as long as only cavalry attacked.

claims.value: Side A attacked and pursued: Dupont's infantry drove side B from the wood near Albeck, the light cavalry and Klein's dragoons charged and pursued it toward Eselsburg, and at night the 9e léger, with the Guard chasseurs and the 20e dragons, carried Herbrechtingen. Side B retreated, turning to face its pursuers, and stood on the heights of Herbrechtingen to hold them up.
claims.rationale: All the accounts read describe side A attacking and pursuing a retreating side B; side B's stand at Herbrechtingen was defensive. The phase is left unresolved: Napoleon's verbal order to beat and pursue and Berthier's order to Dupont to attack set the day's offensive, while Murat's letter shows him deciding the night attack on Herbrechtingen itself (claim side-a-command), and Bodart's entry does not say whether it covers the day or the night action. English renderings (ours): Alombert and Colin, 'Dupont swiftly drives the enemy from the wood bordering the road; the Austrian cavalry then makes a retrograde movement on Nerenstetten, and Murat takes advantage of it to have it charged'; Krauss, as in claims side-a-command, means-and-supply and side-b-command; Murat, 'I resolved to drive the enemy from Herbrechtingen'; Alombert and Colin, as in claim bodart-winner.

claims.value: Krauss places Werneck's troops on the heights of Herbrechtingen and has Dupont's light infantry regiment take Herbrechtingen after a short fight. He names no walls or other works.
claims.rationale: none_named reports the passages read, not proof that no works existed; the dragoon division's journal, coded separately, names a crenellated wall (claim fortification-french-accounts). English renderings (ours): 'Werneck now drew up his troops on the heights of Herbrechtingen'; 'which after a short fight took Herbrechtingen'.

open_questions: Deferred: Murat's letter and the 1st dragoon division's journal were read only as Alombert and Colin print them; Dupont's division journal and General Mouton's report, which they cite for Berthier's lost order; Werneck's relation and report (Kriegsarchiv), which Krauss quotes; Krauss's map (Beilage 31). Figures seen only in the OCR and not recorded: the cavalry taken with their horses in the charges (Murat's letter, Alombert and Colin, t. III, vol. 2, p. 1200).

Most consequential gap: side B's strength in the action. No Austrian return for Werneck's corps was read: Krauss gives battalions and squadrons for the 15th and scarcely 6000 men for the 17th, after this action; side A's information gave about 8,000 for the rearguard; Bodart's 4,000 lies below both, and none of them says which of Werneck's troops fought on the 16th. A strength return of Werneck's corps in Krauss's appendices or the Kriegsarchiv files could close it. Side A's force is also uncertain: the returns read are three weeks older than the action and the Guard chasseurs' strength was not found.

Disputes kept as separate claims or recorded in them: side B's commander as Hohenzollern (Bodart) or Werneck (Krauss, Dupont's parlementaire), with Hohenlohe for the corps in Conchy's information; the hour of the night attack, 9 in the evening (journal, Krauss) or 11 (Murat); O'Donell marked with Bodart's dagger, against the journal's O'Donnel wounded and taken; side B's loss as about 2,500 men and 2 flags (Bodart) or about 3,000 taken, 300 killed and 200 wounded (journal); the parley as opened by Dupont (Murat, Alombert and Colin) or ordered by Murat (journal); the two chasseur regiments as drawn in by Murat (Krauss) or come with Oudinot's grenadiers (Alombert and Colin); Herbrechtingen as a village (Bodart, Alombert and Colin) or a small town with a crenellated wall (journal).

Families and dependence: Bodart (a compilation; his sources for this entry were not checked); Alombert and Colin, t. II and t. III (the French official history, printing the returns, Murat's letter and the 1st dragoon division's journal, interested accounts, and Conchy's information); Krauss (an Austrian history drawing on Werneck's relation and report and on the French documents; his account of the French side is not treated as independent of Alombert and Colin).
